text: section time questions what it contains listening 30 minutes 40 four recordings, each heard once only reading 60 minutes 40 three sections, no extra transfer time writing 60 minutes 2 tasks a letter of 150 words, an essay of 250 words speaking 11 to 14 min 3 parts a face to face interview with an examiner listening and speaking are identical in the academic and general training versions. only reading and writing are different, and that difference works in your favour: the texts are shorter and the letter is easier to learn than a data description.

in listening and reading, one correct answer is worth one mark, out of 40. that raw score is then converted into a band from 1 to 9. writing and speaking are marked by trained examiners against four published criteria each. raw score to band this is the part most students do not know, and it changes how you should work. general training reading needs more correct answers than academic reading for the same band, because the texts are easier. band listening, out of 40 gt reading, out of 40 academic reading, for comparison 4 10 15 10 5 16 23 15 6 23 30 23 7 30 34 30 8 35 38 35 read that table again the gap between band 5 and band 6 in reading is seven answers. seven questions stand between you and your target. most students lose those seven not because they failed to understand the text, but because they left blanks, wrote too many words, or spelled the answer wrongly. your overall band the overall band is the average of the four sections, rounded to the nearest half. if you score 6 in listening, 5.5 in reading, 5 in writing and 6 in speaking, the total is 22.5, the average is 5.625, and the reported band is 5.5. an average ending in .25 rounds up to the next half band; an average end

sectionTitle: Ten rules that apply to the whole test
text: never leave a blank. a wrong answer costs nothing. a blank is a guaranteed zero. spelling is part of the answer. a correct word spelled wrongly scores nothing. singular and plural are part of the answer. if the text says books and you write book, you lose the mark. obey the word limit. if the instruction says two words maximum, three words scores zero even when the meaning is right. write in capital letters in listening and reading. this removes any doubt about proper nouns and makes your handwriting readable. answer the question asked, not the topic. what you personally know about the subject is not a source of answers. copy the spelling from the text. if the word is printed in front of you, there is no excuse for getting it wrong. watch your own clock. nobody warns you about time in reading or writing. do not change an answer unless you have a reason. your first reading of a question is usually the more careful one. transfer as you go. in reading there is no extra minute at the end to copy answers across.

bring the same id document you registered with. without it you will not be admitted. no paper, no phone, no notes go into the room. in listening, use the reading time you are given to read ahead. it is part of the strategy, not a rest. in reading, write answers straight onto the answer sheet as you work. in writing, start with task 2 if you are worried about time. it is worth twice as much as task 1. if you miss a listening question, guess immediately and move on. stopping costs you the next two questions as well.

recording type context level 1 conversation between two people everyday life: booking, enquiring, registering easiest 2 one speaker everyday life: a tour, instructions, an announcement easy 3 two to four people educational: discussing an assignment or project harder 4 one speaker an academic talk or lecture hardest each recording carries 10 questions. the questions always follow the order of the recording. if you are hunting for question 5 and you hear something that belongs to question 6, then question 5 has gone. leave it, guess, and move forward. students who refuse to let go of one question lose three.

word limits instruction what it allows one word only one word. no number. no more than two words one or two words. no number. no more than two words and/or a number up to two words, and a number may be added. no more than three words and/or a number up to three words, and a number may be added. a hyphenated word such as well-known counts as one word. a figure such as 240 counts as a number, not a word. a, an and the all count as words. leave them out when you are close to the limit. numbers, dates and money long numbers are said digit by digit: 050 447 2913 is said as zero five zero, four four seven, two nine one three. double and triple mean a repeated digit. double four is 44. triple eight is 888. dates may be written in any clear form: 12 march, march 12 and 12/3 are all accepted. do not repeat a word that is already printed. if the form says aed and you hear two hundred and forty dirhams, write 240. spelling traps when a speaker spells something out letter by letter, that is always because the word is the answer. these are the letter pairs that cost arabic speakers the most marks. pair how to tell them apart b / p b has voice in it. p is a puff of air with no voice. g / j g is

sectionTitle: Question type 1: form, note and table completion
text: this is most of recording 1, it is the easiest question type in the test, and it is where careless students throw away the most marks. you fill a gap in a form, a table or a set of notes. the method use the reading time. read every gap before the recording starts. predict the type of answer for each gap: a name, a number, a date, an amount, a place, a day. write a one-word reminder above the gap. read the words around the gap. those words are what you will hear just before the answer, so they are your warning signal. write exactly what you hear. do not rephrase it and do not correct the speaker's grammar. if the speaker repeats or corrects themselves, the answer is the correction, not the first version. when the recording ends, check spelling, singular or plural, and the word limit. the most common trap in this type the speaker gives a piece of information and then takes it back. for example: the fee is three hundred dirhams, sorry, that was last year, it is now two hundred and forty. the answer is 240. your ear catches the first number; the test rewards the student who stays with the sentence to the end. practice 1 your teacher will read a telephone conversation once only. you hav

you hear a question and choose one of three options. this is the most dangerous type in the listening section, because the recording usually mentions all three options and rules two of them out quickly. how the wrong options are built the examiner builds distractors in three predictable ways. learn to recognise them and half the difficulty disappears. the option is mentioned, but it belongs to a different person, a different place or a different time. the option was true and then the speaker rejected it or changed their mind. the option repeats the exact words from the recording, while the correct answer uses a synonym. this one catches every student who listens for words instead of meaning. the method read the stem first, the part before the options, and be clear about what is being asked. underline the one or two words that actually separate the three options from each other. listen for meaning, not for whichever option is mentioned first. cross an option out with your pencil the moment it is ruled out. do not try to hold it in your head. if you lose the question, choose any option at once and move on. never go back. a practical warning the first option mentioned in the recording

sectionTitle: Question type 3: map and plan labelling
text: you are given a map or a floor plan and you label the places on it. students are afraid of this type, but it is the easiest one in the section once you know about twenty words. direction vocabulary you must know by heart expression meaning opposite / facing directly across from next to / beside / adjacent to at the side of between with one thing on each side behind / in front of at the back of, at the front of at the end of at the far point of a corridor or road at the top / bottom of at the upper or lower part turn left / right change direction go straight on / carry on continue without turning on your left / right on that side as you walk the first / second turning the first or second road you can turn into in the corner where two walls meet entrance / exit way in, way out ground floor / first floor the floor at street level, the floor above it upstairs / downstairs on a higher or lower floor along following the length of something across from on the other side of just past slightly beyond immediately after the very next one in the far corner in the corner furthest from you halfway along at the middle point the method find your starting point before the recording begins. it is us

you are given a list of items and a list of options, and you connect them. for example, five people and five opinions, or five buildings and five uses. the method read the option list first and understand it properly. it will be said in the recording with different words. write a short code next to each option so that you can write it quickly while listening. follow the order of the items. it matches the order of the recording. check whether the instructions allow an option to be used more than once. guess any option you did not hear rather than leaving it empty.

sectionTitle: Question type 5: sentence completion and short answer
text: you complete a sentence or answer a question in a few words. the grammar of the sentence around the gap is your best clue and most students ignore it. the method read the whole sentence, including the part after the gap. decide the grammar of the missing word: is it a noun, a verb, an adjective, a plural? if the word before the gap is a or an, the answer is a singular noun. if it is are or were, the answer is plural. listen for the meaning of the whole sentence, not for the individual words printed on your paper. read your completed sentence back. if it is not grammatical english, your answer is wrong even if the word was in the recording. grammar as a checking tool if the sentence reads: the centre was built to provide ................ for local families, then the gap needs a noun, and most likely an uncountable or plural noun because there is no article in front of it. you have narrowed the answer down before you have heard a single word.

four sessions a week of twenty minutes each will do far more for you than one long session. session what you do 1 do a full listening section under test conditions: once only, no pausing, no translating. 2 mark it, then listen again with the script in front of you and mark every point where you went wrong. 3 listen only to the parts you got wrong, again and again, until you can hear the word clearly. 4 write twenty new words from the recording into your notebook with their pronunciation, and review them the next day.

general training reading has three sections and 40 questions in 60 minutes. the texts come from the kind of english you would meet in daily life: notices, advertisements, timetables, staff handbooks, company guidelines, newspapers and magazines. section texts what they are questions 1 two or three short texts social survival: advertisements, notices, timetables, instructions about 14 2 two short texts workplace: job descriptions, contracts, staff handbooks, training material about 13 3 one long text general interest: a magazine or newspaper article about 13 the scoring warning again because these texts are easier than the academic ones, the conversion is harder. you need 30 correct out of 40 for band 6, and 34 for band 7. accuracy matters more than speed here. a student who finishes in 45 minutes with 26 correct scores lower than one who uses all 60 minutes and gets 31.

there is no extra time at the end to copy your answers across. write them on the answer sheet as you work. section time to spend why 1 15 minutes short texts, direct answers. do not linger. 2 20 minutes longer sentences and more careful wording. 3 25 minutes one long text, the hardest question types. if a question takes more than 90 seconds, guess it, circle the number and move on. come back only if time allows. do the question types you are strongest at first within each section. check the clock at the end of each section, not every five minutes.

sectionTitle: The two reading skills you actually need
text: skimming skimming means moving your eyes fast over a text to find out what it is about and how it is organised. you are not reading, you are surveying. give a long text 60 seconds: read the title, the first sentence of each paragraph, and any words in bold or capitals. that is enough to build a map. scanning scanning means hunting for one specific thing: a name, a date, a figure, a place. your eyes move in zigzags down the page and ignore everything that is not the shape of what you want. numbers, capital letters and unusual words are the easiest things to scan for, which is why questions containing them are the quickest to answer. do those first. the paraphrase problem the answer in the text almost never uses the same words as the question. this is the single most important fact about ielts reading. before you go hunting, spend three seconds asking: how else could this idea be written? if the question says the text may say lends equipment available to borrow, provided free, you may take one children under-12s, young people, minors, those aged 5 to 11 is not allowed is prohibited, must not, is restricted, may not costs nothing free of charge, at no cost, complimentary, included emp

sectionTitle: Question type: matching information to a text
text: this is the typical section 1 question. you are given several short texts labelled a, b, c and d, and a list of statements. you decide which text each statement belongs to. how students lose marks here they read all four texts from beginning to end before looking at the questions, and use half their time. these texts are not for reading, they are for searching. you are not reading a newspaper, you are looking up a number in a directory. the method read the question first, never the text. find the key idea in it, usually a noun or a verb that is hard to replace. think of the paraphrase before you search. if the question says lends equipment, look for available to borrow or provided. sweep the texts vertically and quickly, looking for the idea, not the word. read the whole sentence before you write a letter down. most errors come from spotting a similar word and stopping there. mark in the text where you found each answer, so that checking later takes seconds. watch the instructions in this type the same letter can usually be the answer to more than one question. the instruction says: you may use any letter more than once. do not reject a letter just because you have already used it.

sectionTitle: Question type: True, False, Not Given
text: this is where students lose more marks than in any other question type in the paper. it is also completely learnable, because the rule is mechanical. the definitions. learn them exactly. answer when you choose it true the statement agrees with the information in the text, even if different words are used. false the text says something that contradicts the statement. there is something in the text that makes it wrong. not given the text says nothing about this at all, neither confirming it nor denying it. the golden rule false means the text spoke and said the opposite. not given means the text was silent. the question you ask yourself is never is this true in the real world, it is what did this text actually say. your own knowledge of the subject is worth nothing here and will often harm you. power words change the answer words that make a claim absolute or flexible are the hinge on which these questions turn. circle them in every statement before you start. absolute words flexible words all, every, always, never, only, must, none, entirely some, many, may, might, often, usually, generally, tends to if the text says most students and the statement says all students, the answer is f

sectionTitle: Question type: Yes, No, Not Given
text: this looks identical to the previous type but it is not. true, false and not given ask about facts in the text. yes, no and not given ask about the views and claims of the writer. type you are checking typical text true / false / not given factual information rules, notices, procedures, reports yes / no / not given the writer's opinion or claim opinion articles, argument pieces the method is the same, but you are now hunting for opinion language: i believe, it seems clear that, unfortunately, surprisingly, the real problem is, critics argue. when a text is full of such language, expect this question type. careful if the writer reports what someone else thinks, that is not the writer's own view. a sentence such as some economists claim that the policy failed tells you what economists think, not what the writer thinks. a statement about the writer's own view would then be not given.

sectionTitle: Question type: sentence, note, table and flow-chart completion
text: you copy words from the text into a gap. the answer is always a word that appears in the text, and it must be copied exactly. the method check the word limit and write it at the top of the page so you keep seeing it. read the whole sentence including what comes after the gap. decide the grammar of the missing word before you search: noun, verb, adjective, singular, plural. find the part of the text the sentence is based on, using the words around the gap. copy the word exactly as it is spelled in the text. do not change its form. read the finished sentence back. if it is not grammatical, the answer is wrong. two rules students break constantly first: you cannot change the word. if the text says decision and the sentence needs decide, the answer is not the question type you thought it was, so look again. second: you cannot exceed the limit. three words where two are allowed scores zero even if the meaning is perfect.

a short summary of one part of the text, with gaps. it comes in two forms: fill the gaps from the text itself, or choose from a box of given words. the method read the whole summary first to understand what it is about. do not start with gap one. identify which part of the text the summary covers. it is usually one or two paragraphs, not the whole text. predict the grammar and the meaning of each gap before searching. if there is a word box, remember the box always contains more words than gaps, and the extra ones are chosen to look attractive. with a word box, cross words off as you use them so that the choice narrows.

one question, three or four options. slower than other types, so do not start with these. the method read the stem and cover the options with your hand. answer the question from the text in your own words first. now uncover the options and find the one that matches what you said. eliminate actively. cross out an option the moment you can prove it wrong. be suspicious of an option that repeats the exact words of the text. it is usually a distractor. never choose an option because it is true in the real world. choose it because this text says it.

you are given a list of headings and you choose one for each paragraph. there are always more headings than paragraphs. this type appears mainly in section 3. the method do this type first in the section, before the other questions, because it forces you to understand the structure of the whole text. read the headings first and group any that look similar. the examiner puts near-identical headings in the list on purpose. for each paragraph, read the first sentence, the last sentence, and skim the middle. ask what the paragraph is mainly about, not what it mentions. a detail in one line is not the topic. cross off each heading as you use it. do the easy paragraphs first and let elimination solve the hard ones. main idea against detail a paragraph can mention the cost of a project in one sentence while being mainly about its history. the heading the cost of the project would then be wrong. ask yourself: if i removed this sentence, would the paragraph still make sense? if yes, it is a detail, not the main idea.

sectionTitle: Question type: matching features and sentence endings
text: matching features gives you a list of people, places, years or organisations, and a list of statements, and you connect them. matching sentence endings gives you the first half of a sentence and a list of possible endings. the method for matching features scan the text for the names or dates in the option list and underline every one. they are easy to find because they are capitalised or numerical. work through the text in order rather than through the questions in order, because the names are scattered. read the whole sentence around each name before matching. check whether options may be used more than once. the method for sentence endings read the sentence beginning and predict how it should finish. eliminate endings that do not fit grammatically. this alone removes several options. then find the relevant place in the text and confirm the meaning. the beginnings follow the order of the text, so use that to narrow your search.

a direct question with a short answer taken from the text, within a word limit. these are usually the quickest marks in the paper, so find them and do them first. the answer is always words taken from the text, never your own words. question words tell you the answer type: who needs a person, when needs a time, where needs a place, how many needs a number. do not write a full sentence. write only the words needed.

read the passage and answer questions 30 to 40. allow yourself 20 minutes. why cities are planting trees again for most of the twentieth century, the tree was treated by city planners as decoration. roads were widened, car parks were laid, and where a tree stood in the way of either, the tree was removed. in some european and north american cities, the number of street trees fell by more than a third between 1950 and 1990. trees were seen as expensive to maintain, a hazard in storms, and an obstacle to traffic. that view has now reversed almost completely. city governments from melbourne to manchester have set targets to increase the share of land covered by tree canopy, and several have committed to planting a million trees or more. the change is not driven by beauty. it is driven by measurements, and above all by temperature. a street lined with mature trees can be several degrees cooler than an identical street without them, because leaves block sunlight before it reaches the road surface and because water evaporating from the leaves cools the surrounding air. the health evidence has strengthened the case. studies in several countries have found lower rates of heat-related illne

you are given a situation in three or four lines, followed by three bullet points. you write a letter of at least 150 words covering all three bullet points. you have 20 minutes. task 1 is worth one third of your writing band, and task 2 is worth two thirds, so do not spend more than 20 minutes here. what you are marked on criterion what the examiner is looking for task achievement all three bullet points covered, the right tone for the reader, at least 150 words coherence and cohesion clear paragraphs, one idea per paragraph, logical order, linking that is not forced lexical resource a range of appropriate words, spelled correctly, in the right register grammatical range and accuracy a mix of simple and complex sentences, with control of tense and punctuation the cheapest marks in the whole test writing fewer than 150 words is penalised automatically. missing one of the three bullet points is penalised automatically. both are entirely within your control and cost you nothing to fix. count your words once, in week one of your practice, and learn what 150 words looks like in your own handwriting. after that you will never need to count again.

everything in the letter depends on one decision made in the first ten seconds: who am i writing to? get this wrong and even a well written letter loses marks. register who you are writing to signal in the question formal someone you do not know, by role: a manager, a company, a council write to the manager, to the company, to the editor semi-formal someone you know in an official relationship: your landlord, your teacher, your neighbour write to your landlord, your supervisor, your neighbour informal a friend or family member write to a friend, to your cousin, to your former classmate openings and closings, which must match register opening closing formal, name unknown dear sir or madam, yours faithfully, formal, name known dear mr khan, / dear ms adams, yours sincerely, semi-formal dear mr khan, / dear mrs adams, yours sincerely, / best regards, informal dear sara, / hi omar, best wishes, / all the best, / love, never write dear sir or madam and then sign yours sincerely. the pair is fixed. never use a first name with mr or ms. dear mr ahmed is only correct if ahmed is the family name. in an informal letter you may use contractions such as i'm and don't. in a formal letter, write

sectionTitle: The structure that works every time
text: five paragraphs, each doing one job. this structure fits every letter type and takes the thinking out of the exam room. paragraph job length opening greeting and one sentence saying why you are writing 1 sentence body 1 bullet point one, developed with a detail or example 3 to 4 sentences body 2 bullet point two, developed 3 to 4 sentences body 3 bullet point three, developed 3 to 4 sentences closing what you want to happen next, and the sign-off 1 to 2 sentences develop, do not just mention the difference between band 5 and band 6 in this task is almost always development. band 5 answers say what happened. band 6 answers say what happened, and then add one sentence of detail, reason or consequence. if a bullet point takes you one sentence, you have not finished it.

saying why you are writing formal informal i am writing to enquire about ... i'm writing to ask about ... i am writing to complain about ... i wanted to let you know about ... i am writing with regard to ... i thought i'd write and tell you about ... i am writing to request ... just a quick note about ... i am writing to apply for the position of ... guess what happened last week! making a request formal informal i would be grateful if you could ... could you do me a favour and ...? would it be possible for you to ...? is there any chance you could ...? i would appreciate it if you could ... do you think you could ...? i would like to request that ... any chance of ...? complaining i am afraid i was extremely disappointed with ... unfortunately, the service did not meet the standard i had expected. the problem was made worse by the fact that ... i trust you will understand my frustration in this matter. apologising i would like to apologise for ... (formal) please accept my sincere apologies for the inconvenience caused. (formal) i'm really sorry about ... (informal) i feel awful about missing it. (informal) explaining a reason this was due to ... / this was caused by ... the reaso

formal letter template dear sir or madam, i am writing to [state your purpose in one line]. [bullet 1 topic sentence]. [detail]. [consequence or example]. [bullet 2 topic sentence]. [detail]. [consequence or example]. [bullet 3 topic sentence]. [detail]. [what you want done]. i look forward to hearing from you. yours faithfully, [your full name] informal letter template dear [first name], thanks for your last letter. i'm writing to tell you about [purpose]. [bullet 1]. [detail]. [feeling or reaction]. [bullet 2]. [detail]. [feeling or reaction]. [bullet 3]. [detail]. [invitation or question back to them]. anyway, that's all my news. write back soon and tell me how you are. best wishes, [your first name]

task a, formal the question you recently stayed at a hotel and were not satisfied with your room. write a letter to the hotel manager. in your letter: • explain when you stayed and which room you had • describe the problems you experienced • say what you would like the manager to do write at least 150 words. model answer, 176 words dear sir or madam, i am writing to complain about the standard of the room i was given during my recent stay at your hotel. i stayed at the marina branch from 3 to 6 september and was allocated room 412 on the fourth floor. i had booked a quiet double room with a sea view, and this was confirmed in writing when i made the reservation two months earlier. unfortunately, the room did not match that description in several respects. it faced the main road rather than the sea, and the traffic noise continued until well after midnight, which made it almost impossible to sleep. in addition, the air conditioning produced a loud rattling sound whenever it started, and although i reported this twice at reception, nobody came to look at it during the three days i was there. i would therefore be grateful if you could refund the difference between the room i booked an

write each of these in 20 minutes, by hand, with a timer. do not look anything up while writing. you borrowed a book from a friend and damaged it. write to your friend: apologise, explain what happened, say what you will do about it. you want to take an evening course at a local college. write to the college: say which course you are interested in, ask about the timetable and fees, explain why you want to take it. your neighbour has been carrying out building work that is disturbing you. write to your neighbour: describe the problem, explain the effect it is having, suggest a solution. you recently attended a training day at work that you found useful. write to your manager: say which parts were useful, explain how you will apply them, suggest what could be improved. a friend is visiting your country next month. write to your friend: say what the weather will be like, suggest what to bring, recommend two places to visit. you ordered a product online and it arrived damaged. write to the company: give the order details, describe the damage, say what you want them to do.

run through this list every time you finish a letter. ten of these items cost nothing and save marks. did i cover all three bullet points? is my letter at least 150 words? does my opening match my closing? have i used contractions in a formal letter by mistake? does each paragraph have one clear job? did i develop each point with a detail, a reason or a consequence? have i begun every sentence with a capital letter and ended it with a full stop? have i checked the spelling of the words i always get wrong? is my handwriting readable to a stranger? did i finish in 20 minutes?

you are given a statement and a question about it, and you write an essay of at least 250 words in 40 minutes. this task carries twice the marks of task 1, so it deserves twice the time and should be done first if you are worried about the clock. criterion what the examiner is looking for task response you answer the exact question asked, take a clear position, and support it coherence and cohesion clear paragraphing, logical progression, linking that fits the meaning lexical resource range and precision of vocabulary, including some less common words used correctly grammatical range and accuracy variety of structures and control of them, including punctuation the single biggest cause of a low task 2 score answering the question you wish you had been asked. if the question asks whether the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, an essay listing advantages and disadvantages without ever saying which is greater does not answer it, however good the english is. underline the question, and read it again after your introduction.

type how the question is phrased what you must do opinion to what extent do you agree or disagree? take one clear side and defend it throughout discussion discuss both views and give your own opinion. one paragraph per view, then your own position advantages and disadvantages do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages? both sides, then a clear judgement on which is greater problem and solution what problems does this cause and how can they be solved? problems in one paragraph, solutions in the next two-part question why is this happening? what can be done? answer both parts, one paragraph each

paragraph job words introduction rephrase the topic, then state what your essay will do or what you think 40 to 50 body 1 first main idea: state it, explain it, give an example 80 to 90 body 2 second main idea: state it, explain it, give an example 80 to 90 conclusion restate your position in different words. no new ideas. 35 to 45 the body paragraph formula topic sentence: the main idea in one sentence, with no example in it. explanation: why this is true, in two or three sentences. example: something concrete. it may be from research, from a country, or from ordinary life. link back: one short sentence connecting the idea to the question asked. your examples do not have to be famous you will not be penalised for an example from your own experience or from your own country. a specific, believable example is worth far more than a vague reference to studies that have shown. if you invent a statistic, keep it plausible and general.

opinion essay introduction: it is sometimes argued that [rephrase the statement]. in my view, [state your position clearly, in one sentence]. body 1: the main reason for this is that [first reason]. [explain]. [example]. this suggests that [link back]. body 2: a further consideration is [second reason]. [explain]. [example]. for this reason, [link back]. conclusion: in conclusion, although [acknowledge the other side in half a sentence], i believe that [restate your position in different words]. discussion essay introduction: opinions differ as to whether [rephrase]. this essay will consider both positions before explaining why i believe [your view]. body 1: those who support [view a] argue that [reason]. [explain]. [example]. body 2: on the other hand, supporters of [view b] point out that [reason]. [explain]. [example]. conclusion: having considered both views, i am persuaded that [your view], primarily because [one reason]. advantages and disadvantages introduction: [rephrase the topic]. while this development brings certain benefits, i would argue that the drawbacks are more significant. body 1: the clearest advantage is that [benefit]. [explain]. [example]. body 2: however, th

sectionTitle: Linking phrases that are worth using
text: function phrases adding furthermore, in addition, moreover, what is more contrasting however, on the other hand, nevertheless, while it is true that giving reasons this is because, the main reason is that, owing to, as a result of showing results consequently, as a result, this means that, therefore giving examples for instance, to take one example, this can be seen in conceding admittedly, it is certainly true that, although some may argue concluding in conclusion, to sum up, having considered both sides linking words are seasoning, not food starting every sentence with moreover or firstly lowers your score rather than raising it. examiners describe this as mechanical. two or three well placed linkers in a paragraph is plenty. the strongest cohesion comes from ideas following each other logically, not from the words glued between them.

sectionTitle: Two answers to the same question, compared
text: the question some people believe that mobile phones should be banned in schools. others think they are a useful learning tool. discuss both views and give your own opinion. write at least 250 words. answer a, around band 5.5 nowadays mobile phone is very important in our life. some people think it should be banned in school and other people think it is good for learning. in this essay i will discuss both view and give my opinion. firstly, some people think mobile phone should be banned because student use it in the class and they don't listen to teacher. also they can cheat in the exam by using internet. moreover they can be addicted and this is bad for their health. so the teacher cannot control the class. secondly, other people think mobile phone is useful tool. because student can search information quickly and they can use many application for study. moreover if there is emergency the parent can call them. so it is useful. in conclusion, i think mobile phone has advantage and disadvantage. both view are correct. school should decide what is better for them. what is holding answer a back task response: the conclusion gives no opinion. saying both views are correct is not a posit

write each of these in 40 minutes, by hand, with a timer. plan for five minutes before you start writing. some people think that young people should be required to do unpaid community work. to what extent do you agree or disagree? in many countries, people are working longer hours than in the past. what are the causes of this, and what effects does it have? some believe governments should spend money on public transport rather than on building new roads. discuss both views and give your own opinion. more and more people are choosing to live alone. do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages? many young people leave their home towns to find work in large cities. what problems does this cause, and how could they be reduced? some people think that examinations are a poor way of measuring what a student has learned. to what extent do you agree or disagree?

sectionTitle: The ten mistakes that cost the most marks
text: not answering the exact question asked. no clear position, or a position that changes between the introduction and the conclusion. writing fewer than 250 words. one long paragraph, or paragraphs that contain two unrelated ideas. listing ideas without explaining or exemplifying any of them. memorised sentences that do not fit the topic. examiners recognise them immediately. starting every sentence with a linking word. repeating the words of the question instead of rephrasing them. introducing a brand new idea in the conclusion. running out of time and leaving the essay unfinished. an unfinished essay is heavily penalised.

part length what happens 1 introduction and interview 4 to 5 minutes the examiner asks familiar questions about you: home, work, study, hobbies 2 long turn 3 to 4 minutes you get a card with a topic, one minute to prepare, then you speak for 1 to 2 minutes 3 discussion 4 to 5 minutes broader, more abstract questions connected to the part 2 topic criterion what it means in practice fluency and coherence can you keep going at a natural pace, and do your ideas connect? lexical resource do you have the words you need, and can you get around the ones you lack? grammatical range and accuracy do you use more than one tense and more than one sentence shape, correctly? pronunciation can you be understood without effort? what is not marked you are not marked on your opinions, on how interesting your life is, or on having a british accent. you may invent an answer entirely. the examiner is listening to your english, not checking your facts. a student who says nothing because nothing interesting has happened to them is scoring zero for honesty.

the questions are short and personal. the danger here is the one-word answer. if you answer in three words, the examiner moves on and you lose the chance to show what you can do. the three-part answer every part 1 answer should have three moves. practise this until it is automatic. answer the question directly. give a reason or a detail. add an example, a contrast, or something about the past or the future. the same question, two ways q: do you enjoy cooking? weak answer: yes, i like it. strong answer: yes, i do, though mainly at the weekend. during the week i get home late and i usually just heat something up, but on fridays i like to take my time and cook something properly. last week i tried making a levantine lentil soup that my grandmother used to make, and it actually turned out quite well. part 1 question bank home: where do you live? do you prefer living in a house or a flat? what do you like about your neighbourhood? would you like to move? work and study: what do you do? why did you choose that subject? what is the most difficult part of it? what would you like to do in the future? free time: what do you do in your free time? has this changed since you were a child? do yo

you are given a card with a topic and three or four prompts. you have one minute to prepare and then you must speak for one to two minutes without interruption. how to use the one minute do not write sentences. write single words only, four or five of them. write one word for each prompt on the card, plus one extra idea. decide the tense before you start: most cards are about a past experience, so plan to use the past simple. decide your ending sentence now, so you never stop awkwardly. if you have no real experience of the topic, invent one. it costs nothing and no one checks. structure of the long turn follow the prompts on the card in order. they are a plan, and using them guarantees you cover enough. then add one extra sentence beyond the last prompt, because that is where the card usually asks you to explain, and that explanation is where the higher marks live. sample cue card describe a skill you learned that has been useful to you. you should say: • what the skill is • when and how you learned it • how difficult it was to learn and explain why it has been useful to you. model long turn the skill i want to talk about is touch typing, which basically means typing without looki

the questions become general and abstract. you are no longer talking about yourself, you are talking about people, society, and the future. this is where most students drop half a band, because they keep answering personally. personal against general q: why do some people find it hard to learn new skills as adults? weak answer: for me it is hard because i am busy with work. strong answer: i think there are two main reasons. the obvious one is time: adults have jobs and families, so they cannot give a new skill the hours a child can. but i suspect the bigger reason is psychological. children are used to being bad at things, whereas adults are not, and being visibly bad at something in front of other people is uncomfortable. that discomfort makes people quit early, before they get to the point where it becomes rewarding. useful structures for part 3 function phrases generalising on the whole, in most cases, generally speaking, as a rule hedging it tends to be the case that, i would imagine that, it is probably true that comparing past and present it used to be that, whereas in the past, these days, compared with a generation ago speculating about the future i expect we will see, it i

sectionTitle: Pronunciation: five things that matter most
text: word stress. english words have one strong syllable. say photograph, photographer, photographic. getting the stress wrong can make a familiar word unrecognisable. sentence stress. stress the words that carry meaning, not the small grammar words. final consonants. arabic speakers often drop or soften the end of a word. the difference between want and wanted, or work and worked, lives at the end of the word. the p sound. it exists in english and must be produced with a puff of air. practise pairs: pin and bin, pack and back, cap and cab. pausing. pause at the end of an idea, not in the middle of a phrase. where you pause tells the listener how your sentence is organised.

arabic has no exact equivalent of a and an, so they are the most commonly omitted words in student writing. rule example use a or an for a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time i bought a laptop yesterday. use the when both speaker and reader know which one is meant the laptop i bought is already broken. use the with things there is only one of the sun, the internet, the government use no article for plurals and uncountable nouns in general statements students need support. water is expensive here. use an before a vowel sound, not a vowel letter an hour, an honest man, a university, a european city

english fixes the order subject, verb, object, and puts adjectives before the noun. arabic allows more freedom, and that freedom carries across. wrong right went he to the shop. he went to the shop. i bought a car red. i bought a red car. explain me the rule. explain the rule to me. in my country there is many people. in my country there are many people. i know what is the problem. i know what the problem is.

these nouns are uncountable in english even though their arabic equivalents can be counted. they never take a plural s and never take a or an. uncountable say this instead information a piece of information, some information advice a piece of advice, some advice equipment a piece of equipment furniture an item of furniture research a study, some research news a piece of news (and news takes a singular verb: the news is good) traffic, luggage, money, work, homework, progress no plural form at all

tense use it for example present simple facts, habits, general truths the centre opens at six. present continuous now, or a temporary situation i am staying with my cousin this month. past simple a finished action at a finished time i moved here in august. present perfect a past action with a present result, or no stated time i have lived here for two months. past continuous a background action interrupted by another i was cooking when the power went off. future with will a decision made now, a prediction i will send you the details tomorrow. going to a plan made before now i am going to apply next year. the most common tense error using the present perfect with a finished time expression. i have moved here in august is wrong, because in august is a finished time; write i moved here in august. use the present perfect only when the time is unfinished or unstated: i have lived here since august, or i have already applied.

sectionTitle: Prepositions that cause the most trouble
text: correct common error depend on depend from interested in interested about arrive in a city, arrive at a building arrive to discuss something discuss about something married to someone married with someone responsible for responsible about suffer from suffer of consist of consist from good at, bad at good in, bad in on monday, in august, at six o'clock in monday, on august

every sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. do not join two complete sentences with a comma. use a full stop, or a linking word. put a comma after an introductory phrase: however, the situation has changed. capitalise names, countries, nationalities, languages, months and days: arabic, september, tuesday. do not use an exclamation mark in task 2. it is too informal for an essay.

section 2 of the reading paper is about work: staff handbooks, contracts, training material, company policies. the language is more careful than in section 1, and the questions reward slow reading. allow 18 minutes for the text and questions below. annual leave: staff handbook, section 4 all permanent employees are entitled to 25 days of paid annual leave in each leave year, which runs from 1 january to 31 december. employees who join part way through the year receive a proportion of this entitlement based on the number of complete months they will work before 31 december. part-time employees receive the same entitlement calculated in hours rather than days. an employee working three days a week, for example, receives fifteen days of leave, not twenty-five. requests for leave should be submitted through the staff portal at least three weeks before the first day of absence. requests made with less notice will still be considered, but the department cannot guarantee that they will be approved. your line manager will normally respond within five working days. if you have not received a response after ten working days, contact the human resources team directly rather than resubmitting

sectionTitle: Reading practice 6: summary completion and matching features
text: allow 20 minutes. the quiet economics of volunteering when governments measure the value of work, they count wages. by that measure, the tens of millions of hours given free to hospitals, schools, sports clubs and food banks every year are worth nothing at all. several national statistics offices have begun to challenge this, publishing estimates that place the annual value of volunteer labour in a mid-sized european country somewhere between eight and twelve billion euros. the figures vary because the method does: some estimate what it would cost to hire someone to do the same job, while others use the average wage the volunteer could have earned in that time. karin bosch, an economist at utrecht, argues that both methods miss the point. in her view, much volunteer work has no paid equivalent, because a paid employee simply would not do it in the same way. a volunteer who sits with a hospital patient for two hours is not a cheap substitute for a nurse; the activity exists because it is unpaid, and the patient knows it. bosch suggests measuring outcomes, such as reduced readmission rates, rather than trying to price the hours. others take a more practical view. daniel achebe, who h

two tasks. 60 minutes. spend about 20 minutes on task 1 and 40 minutes on task 2. writing task 1 you recently took a training course at a college, and you were not satisfied with one part of it. write a letter to the course director. in your letter: • give details of the course you took • explain which part was unsatisfactory and why • say what you would like the college to do write at least 150 words. you do not need to write any addresses. begin your letter as follows: dear sir or madam, writing task 2 some people believe that secondary school students should be taught practical skills such as cooking, budgeting and basic repairs, even if this means less time for traditional academic subjects. to what extent do you agree or disagree? give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. write at least 250 words.
